strengths: Addresses a clear and practically relevant limitation of image-to-video diffusion models: specifying which object an actor should interact with using only a target mask and text prompt, rather than dense motion/structure guidance.

The method is simple and well-motivated: adding a mask channel, introducing a target token, and aligning token cross-attention to the target mask is a plausible and lightweight way to induce target awareness in a pretrained video diffusion model.
The paper includes useful ablations on attention-loss block selection, attention region choice, and loss weight, which support the main design decisions.

Quantitative results show a large improvement in target alignment over the base model and fine-tuned-data baseline, and the user studies provide additional evidence that the gains are perceptible to humans.
The qualitative examples demonstrate meaningful capabilities, especially in scenes with multiple similar objects and in complex target-selection cases where text alone is ambiguous.
The implementation details are reasonably complete, including model variant, LoRA setup, training steps, hardware, inference settings, and planned code/dataset release.
weaknesses: The evaluation benchmark is small: only 50 images, five generations each. This is limited evidence for a broad claim about robust target-aware video generation, especially given the diversity of human-object interactions and scene layouts.

The baselines are relatively weak and somewhat indirect. The main comparisons are CogVideoX, CogVideoX fine-tuned on the same data, and an adapted attention-modulation method. There is no strong comparison to more recent or specialized controllable video models that can use masks, boxes, layouts, or sparse trajectories, even if some adaptation would be needed.

The main automatic metric, Contact Score, relies on an off-the-shelf hand-contact detector and overlap with the initial target mask. This can miss non-hand interactions, confuse hallucinated or shifted objects, and does not fully measure whether the intended action was completed plausibly.

The dataset construction is only partially specified. The paper says masks are obtained with an off-the-shelf segmentation model and captions with CogVLM2, but it is unclear how much manual filtering or correction is used, how noisy the masks/captions are, and whether evaluation scenes or object categories overlap substantially with training data.

The novelty is moderate rather than major. The core idea combines mask conditioning with token-attention supervision, both familiar mechanisms in controllable diffusion; the contribution is mainly a well-targeted application and engineering of these ideas to HOI video generation.

The downstream applications are interesting but mostly qualitative. The zero-shot 3D HOI motion synthesis pipeline depends on pose estimation and imitation learning, includes manual scene alignment, and lacks quantitative evaluation against 3D motion or robotics baselines, so the robotics/planning claims are not strongly established.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence. In particular, statements about using video diffusion as a high-level action planner and generating plausible action cues for robotics are suggestive but not validated with task success, physical feasibility metrics, or real/simulated control benchmarks.

The method may be sensitive to mask quality and target visibility, but failure cases and robustness to noisy masks, small/occluded targets, multiple actors, moving cameras, and out-of-distribution actions are not thoroughly analyzed.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and intuitive problem: specifying which object an actor should interact with in image-to-video generation using a simple target mask rather than dense motion guidance.
The proposed implementation is straightforward and practical, building on CogVideoX with an added mask channel, a [TGT] token, LoRA fine-tuning, and an attention-alignment loss.
The paper includes some useful ablations showing that the attention loss, V2T attention choice, selected blocks, and loss weight affect the target-contact metric.
The qualitative examples communicate the intended use case clearly, especially scenes with multiple similar objects where text-only prompting is ambiguous.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited. Adding a spatial mask condition and supervising cross-attention to align with that mask is a fairly incremental adaptation of known attention-control and mask-conditioning ideas; the paper does not convincingly establish a deeper technical contribution.

The evaluation is too small and narrow for the strength of the claims: the benchmark has only 50 images, five generations per image, and appears curated around cases where the target is visually distinguishable and promptable.

The baselines are weak. The main comparisons are the base model, the same model fine-tuned on the data, and a simple attention-modulation adaptation. The paper does not compare against stronger region/mask-conditioned video editing or image-to-video control methods in a quantitatively fair way, despite making broad claims about existing controllable video generation.

The Contact Score is a fragile proxy for successful interaction. It only checks whether an off-the-shelf hand/object contact detector overlaps the target mask in at least one frame, which can reward accidental overlap and does not verify action correctness, temporal plausibility, grasp quality, object state changes, or semantic success.

The user study details are insufficient for strong evidence: the number of unique videos/questions per participant is small, statistical uncertainty is not reported, and the preference table reports only aggregate wins without confidence intervals or significance analysis.

The dataset contribution is underdeveloped. The training set has only 1290 clips, masks are obtained with an off-the-shelf segmenter, captions are automatically generated, and there is limited information about annotation quality, train/test separation from BEHAVE/Ego-Exo4D, possible leakage, or diversity.

Several claims are overstated. The paper frames the model as useful for high-level action planning and zero-shot 3D HOI motion synthesis, but the downstream robotics/physics results are essentially pipeline demonstrations using off-the-shelf pose extraction and imitation learning, with no quantitative task success or physical-interaction evaluation.

The method is likely brittle outside the curated setting: it depends on accurate target masks, static camera data, human-object interaction patterns seen in limited datasets, and the base video model's ability to invent plausible motion. These limitations are acknowledged only partially.

Video quality results are mixed. The proposed method improves target metrics but reduces motion smoothness substantially relative to baselines in Table 1, and the average VBench score is not better than the fine-tuned baseline.

Reproducibility is incomplete at submission time: code and dataset are promised but not available, and important details about evaluation data, prompt refinement, mask generation, and user-study sampling are not sufficient to independently reproduce the main numbers.

strengths: The paper addresses a clear and practically important gap in controllable image-to-video generation: specifying which object an actor should interact with using only a target mask and text prompt, without dense motion or trajectory guidance.

The proposed mechanism is simple and well-motivated: adding a mask condition plus a [TGT]-token cross-attention alignment loss is technically plausible, easy to integrate into existing diffusion-transformer I2V models, and supported by intuitive qualitative evidence.

The evaluation shows consistent gains in target alignment over the base CogVideoX model, fine-tuning-on-data baseline, and an attention-modulation baseline, with especially strong improvements in contact score and human evaluation.
The ablations on loss weight, selected transformer blocks, and attention regions are useful and directly support the main design choices.

The paper includes interesting demonstrations beyond the core benchmark, including multiple same-class objects, non-human subjects, actor-and-target specification, video content creation, and zero-shot 3D HOI motion synthesis.
weaknesses: The quantitative evaluation is relatively small: only 50 benchmark images with five generations each. For a top-tier venue, the central target-alignment claim would be stronger with larger, more diverse, and more systematically stratified evaluation across object categories, actions, scene complexity, and target ambiguity.

The baselines are somewhat limited. The paper argues that dense-control methods are not directly comparable, but stronger adaptations of recent mask-, drag-, layout-, or grounding-based video control methods would be important to establish competitiveness beyond relatively simple baselines.

The Contact Score metric is only a proxy for successful interaction and depends on an off-the-shelf contact detector. It may not distinguish plausible manipulation from accidental overlap, and the paper does not provide enough validation of this metric against human judgments or failure modes.

The downstream applications are compelling but mostly qualitative. The 3D HOI motion synthesis pipeline in particular is not quantitatively evaluated for physical plausibility, task success, contact realism, or comparison to specialized motion-synthesis methods.

The method depends on a curated HOI dataset of 1290 clips, but the dataset construction, filtering criteria, action/category distribution, and potential train-test overlap or bias are not described in enough detail to fully assess generalization.

The novelty is solid but somewhat incremental: mask conditioning plus cross-attention supervision is a natural extension of prior attention-control and controllable diffusion ideas. The main contribution is the adaptation to target-aware HOI video generation rather than a fundamentally new modeling paradigm.

The paper acknowledges video quality limitations, but the reported VBench scores show some tradeoff in motion smoothness and image quality relative to the base model; the qualitative examples also suggest dependence on relatively favorable cases.

Reproducibility is promising due to the stated intent to release code and data, but as submitted it relies on unreleased curated data and several off-the-shelf components whose exact behavior and preprocessing details may affect results.

strengths: Addresses a clear and useful gap in image-to-video generation: specifying which object an actor should interact with using a simple target mask rather than dense motion, trajectory, or structural controls.

The method is technically simple but well motivated: adding a mask channel alone is shown to be insufficient, while the [TGT] token cross-attention alignment loss provides a plausible mechanism for spatial grounding.

Empirical results are fairly convincing within the proposed benchmark: strong gains in Contact Score and human evaluation over vanilla CogVideoX, data-only fine-tuning, and an attention-modulation baseline, while preserving comparable VBench-style video quality.
Includes useful ablations on attention regions, transformer block selection, loss weight, mask quality, and mask shape, supporting several key design choices.

The paper is clearly written and includes substantial qualitative examples, failure cases, implementation details, and downstream demonstrations for 3D HOI motion synthesis and long-form video creation.
weaknesses: The main evaluation benchmark is small: 80 images with 5 generations each. This limits confidence in generalization across diverse scenes, objects, actions, camera motion, and actor-target configurations.

Baseline coverage is somewhat narrow. The paper argues that dense-control methods are not directly comparable, but stronger comparisons to grounded/video editing, mask-conditioned I2V variants, or alternative ways of injecting target masks would make the evidence more compelling.

The primary automatic metric depends on an off-the-shelf human-hand contact detector and initial-frame target masks, which can both misestimate true interaction success. The appendix acknowledges limitations, but the headline results still rely heavily on this imperfect proxy.

The downstream applications are interesting but mostly qualitative. Claims about motion planning, physical plausibility, and robotics relevance would be stronger with quantitative task success, physical-contact/object-motion metrics, or policy evaluation.

Novelty is moderate rather than high: the core recipe combines mask conditioning, a special token, and cross-attention supervision, all of which are natural extensions of existing controllable diffusion ideas.

The dataset curation details are incomplete for reproducibility: only 1290 clips are used, with masks from an off-the-shelf segmenter and captions from a captioning model, but the paper does not fully specify release plans, annotation quality control, train/test separation risks, or detailed filtering criteria.

The method has notable scope limitations: single fixed target, difficulty with multi-instance masks and temporal target switching, mostly static-camera data, and limited automatic evaluation for non-human or robotic actors.

strengths: The paper addresses a clear and useful problem: specifying which object an actor should interact with in image-to-video generation using a target mask and text prompt.

The proposed mechanism is simple and practical: adding a mask channel plus a [TGT]-token cross-attention alignment loss is easy to understand and appears computationally modest relative to the base model.

The manuscript includes several relevant ablations, including attention region choice, transformer block selection, loss weight, and mask perturbations, which help isolate the contribution of the cross-attention loss.
The qualitative examples are broad and visually suggest that the method can improve target grounding in scenes with multiple candidate objects.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is limited. The core contribution is a fairly direct combination of mask conditioning, a special token, and cross-attention supervision, all of which are close to established ideas in controllable diffusion and grounding.

The evaluation is not strong enough to support the paper's broad claims. The main benchmark has only 80 images and 400 generated samples, and it is unclear how diverse, independent, and difficult this benchmark is relative to the curated training data and source datasets.

The baselines are weak and somewhat indirect. Comparing mainly to vanilla CogVideoX, CogVideoX fine-tuned on the same data, and an adapted attention modulation baseline does not establish competitiveness against stronger grounded/interactive video generation, video editing, or mask-conditioned control methods.

The main Contact Score metric is fragile: it relies on an off-the-shelf hand-contact detector, only checks overlap with the initial target mask, and can reward brief or accidental contact. The appendix adds stricter variants, but the evaluation still does not fully capture semantic interaction success, object state change, or temporal correctness.

The downstream application claims are substantially overextended. The robotics and physics-based imitation pipeline is mostly qualitative, uses manually aligned scenes according to the appendix, disables object-motion modules, and does not demonstrate successful closed-loop planning or manipulation.

The paper repeatedly frames the model as a motion planner or world-model-like planner, but the evidence is video generation with target grounding rather than planning under constraints, goal achievement, or physical interaction success.

Reproducibility is incomplete from the manuscript alone: the curated dataset, benchmark split, prompt generation procedure, mask selection, user-study details, and code/model release status are not specified with enough precision to make the results easy to verify.

Several claimed generalizations, such as non-human agents, outdoor scenes, egocentric views, and multiple entities, are supported primarily by cherry-picked qualitative examples rather than systematic evaluation.

The method has important limitations for long-horizon and multi-object interaction: it assumes a fixed target mask, struggles with multiple objects in one mask, and cannot switch targets over time, which undercuts the broader action-planning narrative.

strengths: The paper introduces a clear and useful problem formulation: target-aware image-to-video generation, where a segmentation mask specifies which object the actor should interact with. This is a meaningful control primitive that current text-only I2V models handle poorly, especially with multiple similar objects.

The proposed method is technically simple but well-motivated: adding the target mask as an input channel, introducing a [TGT] token, and supervising the corresponding V2T cross-attention maps provides a plausible mechanism for spatial grounding without requiring dense motion or trajectory annotations.

The empirical results are convincing within the proposed benchmark. The method substantially improves target alignment over CogVideoX, CogVideoX fine-tuned on the same data, and an adapted attention-modulation baseline, with large gains in contact score and human evaluation while maintaining comparable VBench quality metrics.

The ablations are useful and directly support the main design choices, including the importance of the cross-attention loss, V2T attention supervision, selected transformer blocks, loss weight, and robustness to imperfect or coarse masks.

The paper is generally clear, well organized, and includes helpful implementation details such as LoRA setup, training steps, compute, inference settings, and attention-block choices. The dataset curation and automatic-mask experiments also improve the practical credibility of the approach.

The downstream demonstrations for 3D HOI motion synthesis and long-term video creation are compelling as qualitative evidence that target-aware video generation could be useful beyond standalone video synthesis.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is moderate. The core method is a relatively direct combination of mask conditioning, special-token grounding, and cross-attention alignment, so the contribution is more about identifying and validating a useful control interface than introducing a fundamentally new modeling technique.

The evaluation benchmark is fairly small: 80 images with 5 generations each. Although the gains are large, the paper would be stronger with broader testing across more scenes, target categories, action types, camera motions, and out-of-distribution settings.

The baselines are reasonable but not fully satisfying. The paper argues that dense-control methods are not directly comparable, but stronger adaptations of recent video editing, grounding, or instruction-guided video models would make the comparison more definitive.

The main automatic metric relies on a hand-object contact detector and target-mask overlap, which is an imperfect proxy for successful interaction. The authors acknowledge this limitation, especially for non-human or robotic actors, but many headline quantitative claims still depend on this detector.

The downstream applications are mostly qualitative pipeline demonstrations. The robotics/3D HOI claims would be more compelling with quantitative physical success rates, motion realism metrics, or comparisons to existing 3D motion/HOI synthesis methods.

The training data is relatively small and specialized, and the limitations show important constraints: static-camera bias, difficulty with multiple targets in one mask, fixed target specification over time, and scalability issues from requiring extra mask channels per target.

Reproducibility would depend heavily on release of the curated clips, masks, prompts, and evaluation benchmark. The paper gives implementation details, but it is not clear from the manuscript whether all data, code, and evaluation scripts will be released.
